# Glomerular diseases

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Glomerular diseases > Glomerular diseases*

[Original Article Link](/library/mg0VD2)

---

## Summary

<u>Renal glomeruli</u> excrete urinary substances and excess water as an ultrafiltrate into the urine by selectively filtering the blood. Any damage to the <u>glomeruli</u> disrupts the filtration process and results in the appearance of blood components (<u>proteins</u> and <u>red blood cells</u>) in the urine. <u>Glomerular</u> damage is commonly caused by immune-mediated processes, which often lead to <u>glomerulonephritis</u>. Non-inflammatory causes, such as metabolic disease (e.g., <u>diabetes</u>, <u>amyloidosis</u>), can also result in significant damage to the <u>glomeruli</u>. The pathophysiology of <u>glomerular</u> diseases is complex; most patients present with either <u>nephritic syndrome</u> (low-level <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>microhematuria</u>, <u>oliguria</u>, and <u>hypertension</u>) or <u>nephrotic syndrome</u> (high-level <u>proteinuria</u> and generalized <u>edema</u>). All <u>glomerular</u> diseases can progress to acute or <u>chronic renal failure</u>. Thus, quick diagnosis and immediate initiation of therapy are required to prevent irreversible <u>kidney</u> damage.

---

## Definitions

### Terminology of glomerular diseases




* Primary: a <u>kidney</u> disease specifically affecting the <u>glomeruli</u> (e.g., <u>minimal change glomerulonephritis</u>)

* Secondary: a disease affecting the <u>glomeruli</u> in the context of a systemic disease (e.g., <u>lupus nephritis</u> in <u>SLE</u>) or a disease affecting another organ (e.g., <u>diabetic nephropathy</u>)

* Diffuse: > 50% of <u>glomeruli</u> affected (e.g., <u>diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis</u>)

* Focal: < 50% of <u>glomeruli</u> affected (e.g., <u>focal segmental glomerulosclerosis</u>)

* <u>Global</u>: entire <u>glomerulus</u> is affected

* Segmental: only part of the <u>glomerulus</u> is affected

* Proliferative: an increased number of cells in the <u>glomerulus</u>

* Membranous: thickening of the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u> (e.g., <u>membranous nephropathy</u>)

* <u>Sclerosing</u>: scarring of the <u>glomerulus</u>

* Necrotizing: <u>cell death</u> within the <u>glomerulus</u>

* Crescentic: accumulation of cells such as <u>macrophages</u>, <u>fibroblasts</u>, and <u>epithelial</u> cells in Bowman space

---

## Pathophysiology

* The <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> consists of 3 parts  
1. * Initial segment: <u>Fenestrated glomerular capillary endothelium</u> prevents large <u>proteins</u> from passing through.
2. * Second segment: The <u>glomerular basement membrane</u> (<u>GBM</u>) contains a negative charge produced by <u>heparan sulfate</u>.
3. * Final segment: <u>Visceral</u> <u>epithelial</u> cells produce/maintain the <u>GBM</u> and contain intercellular junctions created by <u>podocytes</u> that prevent further protein loss.

* Damage to the <u>glomeruli</u> → disruption of the <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> → can lead to nephritic or nephrotic syndrome

* See “Pathophysiology” in “<u>Nephritic syndrome</u>.“

* See “Pathophysiology” in “<u>Nephrotic syndrome</u>.“

## Nephritic-nephrotic syndrome

### Nephritic-nephrotic syndrome




* Some diseases that manifest with <u>nephritic syndrome</u> can simultaneously cause nephrotic-range <u>proteinuria</u> (; > 3.5 g/24 h), the main feature of <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>.

* When the criteria for both syndromes are fulfilled, the findings are referred to as mixed nephritic-nephrotic syndrome.

* Most common causes of <u>nephritic-nephrotic syndrome</u>:

* <u>Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis</u>

* Classifying the patient's presentation as nephritic, nephrotic, or mixed nephritic-nephrotic can help narrow down the list of likely differential diagnoses.





### Nephrotic vs. nephritic syndrome [[1]](/library/ROalHk)[[2]](/library/kOamsk)




* <u>Nephritic syndrome</u> and <u>nephrotic syndrome</u> are both common clinical manifestations of <u>glomerular</u> diseases.

* Both syndromes are composed of characteristic clinical (e.g., <u>edema</u>, <u>hypertension</u>) and laboratory findings (e.g., <u>glomerular hematuria</u>, massive <u>proteinuria</u>), which result from damage to the <u>glomeruli</u>.

* <u>Glomerular</u> diseases are usually categorized by the syndrome they cause, which is either nephritic or nephrotic.





|  | <u>Nephritic syndrome</u> | <u>Nephrotic syndrome</u> |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Presentation | <br><br>* <u>Proteinuria</u> (< 3.5 g/24 h) (can be in nephrotic range in severe cases )<br><br>* <u>Hematuria</u> with <u>acanthocytes</u><br><br>* <u>RBC casts</u> in urine<br><br>* Mild to moderate <u>edema</u><br><br>* <u>Oliguria</u><br><br>* <u>Azotemia</u><br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br>* <u>Sterile pyuria</u><br><br>* <u>Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis</u> (<u>RPGN</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Heavy <u>proteinuria</u> (> 3.5 g/24 h)<br><br>* <u>Hypoalbuminemia</u><br><br>* Generalized <u>edema</u><br><br>* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u> and <u>fatty casts</u> in urine → frothy urine<br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br>* ↑ Risk of <u>thromboembolism</u>: (via loss of <u>antithrombin III</u>)<br><br>* ↑ Risk of infection (via loss of <u>IgG</u> and tissue <u>edema</u> which compromises the local blood supply and <u>immune response</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Pathophysiology | <br>* Inflammatory response within <u>glomeruli</u> → <u>GBM</u> disruption → loss of renally excreted <u>RBCs</u> (<u>acanthocytes</u>) and ↓ <u>GFR</u> → <u>hematuria</u>, <u>oliguria</u>, <u>azotemia</u>, and ↑ <u>renin</u> → <u>edema</u> and <u>hypertension</u><br><br> | <br>* Damage to <u>podocytes</u> → structural damage of <u>glomerular filtration barrier</u> → massive renal loss of protein<br><br> |
| Causes | <br><br>* <u>Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis</u><br><br>* <u>IgA nephropathy</u> (<u>Berger disease</u>)<br><br>* <u>Granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u><br><br>* <u>Microscopic polyangiitis</u><br><br>* <u>Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u><br><br>* <u>Goodpasture disease</u> (anti-<u>GBM</u> disease)<br><br>* <u>Alport syndrome</u> (<u>hereditary nephritis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Thin basement membrane disease</u><br><br>* <u>Lupus nephritis</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Due to primary or secondary <u>podocyte</u> damage<br><br>* <u>Minimal change disease</u><br><br>* <u>Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis</u><br><br>* <u>Membranous nephropathy</u><br><br>* Due to secondary <u>podocyte</u> damage<br><br>* <u>Diabetic nephropathy</u><br><br>* <u>Amyloid</u> light-chain (AL) <u>amyloidosis</u>, <u>light chain</u> deposition disease<br><br>* <u>Lupus nephritis</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> All <u>glomerular</u> diseases can lead to acute and <u>chronic kidney failure</u>.

## Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)

| <br>Overview of <u>membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis</u> [[3]](/library/QeduAK0)[[4]](/library/VIYGbq)[[5]](/library/sedtZ60)[[6]](/library/Dyc1hU0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | <u>Immunoglobulin</u>-mediated <u>MPGN</u> | <u>Complement</u>-mediated <u>MPGN</u> |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> |  | <br><br>* Rare form of chronic <u>glomerulonephritis</u><br><br>* Most common in children and young adults<br><br><br> |  |
| Definition |  | <br>* Histopathological pattern of <u>glomerular</u> injury characterized by increased number of intraglomerular cells and diffuse thickening of the <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillary</u> walls on <u>light microscopy</u> [[6]](/library/Dyc1hU0)<br><br> |  |
| Pathophysiology |  | <br>* <u>Immune complex</u> deposits → activation of the <u>classical complement pathway</u> → <u>cell injury</u>, mesangial <u>proliferation</u>, and matrix expansion<br><br> | <br>* Intramembranous deposition of <u>complement C3</u> (C3 nephritic factor, an <u>IgG</u> <u>autoantibody</u> that stabilizes <u>C3 convertase</u> and continuously activates C3, leading to its depletion) → activation of the <u>alternative complement pathway</u><br><br> |
| Etiology |  | <br><br>* Primary disease (occurs mainly in children) [[3]](/library/QeduAK0)<br><br>* Secondary disease<br><br>* Infections: <u>HBV</u>, <u>HCV</u><br><br>* Autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>cryoglobulinemia</u>)<br><br>* <u>Malignancy</u>: <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance</u> (<u>MGUS</u>)<br><br>* Hereditary diseases (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>, <u>α1-antitrypsin deficiency</u>)<br><br>* Drugs (e.g., <u>heroin</u>, <u>IFN α</u>)<br><br>* Vascular and clotting disorders (e.g., <u>thrombotic microangiopathy</u>, <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Anomalous regulation of the <u>alternative complement pathway</u> (e.g., <u>dense deposit disease</u>, C3 <u>glomerulonephritis</u>) caused by mutations in (or <u>antibodies</u> to) <u>complement</u> or <u>complement</u> regulatory <u>proteins</u><br><br>* Often associated with a trigger (e.g., infection, <u>MGUS</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Clinical features |  | <br><br>* May manifest with <u>nephritic-nephrotic syndrome</u>, <u>nephritic syndrome</u>, or <u>nephrotic syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Proteinuria</u> (frequently with <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>)<br><br>* <u>Hematuria</u><br><br>* <u>Hypertension</u><br><br>* Abnormal <u>kidney function</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Laboratory studies</u> |  | <br><br>* ↓ Serum <u>C3 complement</u> levels<br><br>* Urianalyisis: nephritic or <u>nephrotic sediment</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <u>Biopsy</u> findings | <br>LM<br> | <br>* H&E or <u>PAS</u> stain shows mesangial ingrowth, which leads to thickening and splitting of the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u> <u>GBM</u> (tram-track appearance).<br><br> |  |
| <br>EM [[3]](/library/QeduAK0)<br> | <br><br>* MPGN type 1: subendothelial and mesangial <u>IgG</u> <u>immune complex</u> deposits with granular appearance<br><br>* <u>MPGN type 2</u>: intramembranous C3 deposits (<u>dense deposit disease</u>) on <u>basement membrane</u><br><br>* <u>MPGN</u> type 3: subendothelial and subepithelial <u>immune complex</u> deposits<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>Management[[6]](/library/Dyc1hU0)<br> |  | <br><br>* Treat the underlying cause<br><br>* <u>Glucocorticoids</u> ± other <u>immunosuppressants</u> (e.g., <u>cyclophosphamide</u>, <u>mycophenolate mofetil</u>)<br><br>* <u>Supportive care</u> (e.g., <u>RAAS inhibitors</u> or other <u>antihypertensives</u>)<br><br>* <u>Complement</u>-targeting therapy (<u>eculizumab</u>) for patients with <u>complement</u> abnormalities whose illness does not respond to other therapies<br><br><br> |  |
| LM = <u>light microscopy</u>, EM = <u>electron microscopy</u><br> |  |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>MPGN</u> is characterized by deposition of <u>antibodies</u> and/or <u>complement factors</u> in the mesangium and along <u>capillary</u> walls.

## Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis

* Definition

* A histopathological pattern of <u>glomerular</u> injury characterized by increased cellularity in > 50% of the <u>glomeruli</u>

* Most common and severe manifestation of <u>lupus nephritis</u> in <u>systemic lupus erythematosus</u> (<u>SLE</u>)

* Also seen in <u>IgA nephropathy</u> and in other inflammatory, autoimmune, and infectious diseases

* Clinical features

* <u>Nephritic syndrome</u>

* <u>Nephritic-nephrotic syndrome</u> (i.e., nephritic with <u>nephrotic-range proteinuria</u>)

* Can lead to <u>immune complex-mediated RPGN</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* ↓ Serum <u>C3 complement</u> levels

* In <u>lupus nephritis</u>: positive <u>ANA</u>, <u>anti-dsDNA</u> <u>antibodies</u>

* Microscopy

* LM

* Thickening of <u>glomerular</u> <u>capillaries</u> (resembling wire loops)

* Characterized by increased cellularity in more than half of the <u>glomeruli</u>

* IM: granular appearance

* EM

* More commonly: subendothelial immune deposits (<u>IgG</u> <u>immune complexes</u>, C3, and <u>C1q</u>)

* Less commonly: subepithelial or intramembranous deposits

* Management: depends on underlying cause





![Lupus nephritis](media/hfpzex193y9o59e3nqc0wgmk.jpg)

Lupus nephritis

## Inherited glomerular disorders

| Overview of <u>inherited glomerular disorders</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | <br><u>Alport syndrome</u>[[7]](/library/MhdMep0) | <br><u>Thin basement membrane disease</u> (<u>benign familial hematuria</u>) [[8]](/library/ABXRW00) |
| <u>Epidemiology</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (∼ 85% <u>X-linked dominant</u>, ∼ 15% <u>autosomal recessive</u>) [[9]](/library/00Xee9)<br><br>* Severe disease typically manifests during <u>adolescence</u>.<br><br>* Most common type of <u>hereditary nephritis</u> (but rare)<br><br><br> | <br>* Affects 5–9% of the general population [[10]](/library/yBXdW00)<br><br> |
| Pathophysiology |  | <br>* Mutation in <u>gene</u> encoding <u>type IV collagen</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Hereditary disorder<br><br>* Abnormalities of <u>type IV collagen</u> causing thinning of <u>GBM</u><br><br><br> |
| Distinguishing features |  | <br><br>* Persistent <u>microhematuria</u> with intermittent <u>gross hematuria</u><br><br>* Associated with sensorineural <u>hearing loss</u>  and abnormalities of the <u>eye</u> (<u>anterior</u> <u>lenticonus</u>, <u>retinopathy</u>)<br><br>* Often leads to <u>ESRD</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Persistent <u>microhematuria</u> and episodic <u>gross hematuria</u> (e.g., following an <u>upper respiratory tract infection</u> or exercise)<br><br>* Good prognosis<br><br><br> |
| <u>Laboratory studies</u> |  | <br><br>* <u>Genetic testing</u> to confirm diagnosis<br><br>* <u>Skin biopsy</u>: alternative test showing absence of <u>collagen type IV</u> alpha 5 chains<br><br>* See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Alport syndrome</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Urinalysis</u>: persistent <u>microhematuria</u><br><br>* <u>Renal biopsy</u> provides definitive diagnosis.<br><br>* See “Diagnostics” in “<u>Thin basement membrane nephropathy</u>.”<br><br><br> |
| <u>Renal biopsy</u> | LM | <br>* Mesangial cell <u>proliferation</u> and <u>sclerosis</u><br><br> | <br>* No abnormalities<br><br> |
| IM | <br>* <u>Collagen IV</u> <u>immunostaining</u> shows absence of <u>collagen IV</u>.<br><br> | <br><br>* Negative Ig and <u>complement</u><br><br>* Occasional trace positivity for <u>IgM</u> and C3 in segmental mesangium<br><br>* Rare trace positivity for <u>IgG</u> and <u>IgA</u> in segmental mesangium<br><br><br> |  |
| EM | <br>* Splitting and alternating thickening and thinning of the <u>GBM</u> (lamellated, basket-weave appearance)<br><br> | <br>* Diffuse thinning of <u>GBM</u><br><br> |  |
| Management |  | <br><br>* Supportive measures to help slow progression of the disease, e.g., <u>ACE inhibitors</u> in patients with <u>proteinuria</u><br><br>* <u>Renal replacement therapy</u> in <u>ESRD</u><br><br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>Alport syndrome</u>.”<br><br><br> | <br><br>* No treatment for <u>isolated hematuria</u><br><br>* <u>ACE inhibitors</u> for patients with <u>proteinuria</u><br><br>* See “Treatment” in “<u>Thin basement membrane nephropathy</u>.”<br><br><br> |
